result.summary: Dionysus appears on a shore as a young man and is seized by Tyrsenian pirates who think he is a king's son. When the ship fills with wine, vines and wild beasts, the pirates leap overboard and become dolphins, while Dionysus spares the helmsman and reveals who he is.

scenes.title: Pirates seize the stranger
scenes.summary: Dionysus appears on a headland as a young man. Pirates capture him, but their bonds fall away and the helmsman realises he is a god.
scenes.stakes: The pirates risk divine anger by binding a god; Dionysus faces no real danger.

place.name: a jutting headland by the shore of the sea

scenes.title: Helmsman warns, master scoffs
scenes.summary: The helmsman urges the crew to free the stranger, whom he takes for a god. The master overrules him and orders the ship to sail on.
scenes.stakes: The crew risk storms and divine wrath if they keep the god captive.

scenes.title: Wonders and transformations aboard
scenes.summary: Wine flows, vines and ivy cover the ship, and Dionysus becomes a lion and conjures a bear. The sailors leap overboard and become dolphins; the helmsman is spared and told who the god is.
scenes.stakes: The sailors lose their human shape and the master his life; the helmsman is at risk but is saved.

scenes.title: Closing salutation
scenes.summary: The poet bids farewell to Dionysus and says no singer should forget him.

alias_notes.explanation: Tyrsenians were the Etruscans, or sea-raiders associated with them, in Greek usage.

notable_quotes.reason: Dionysus reveals his name and parentage to the spared helmsman.
The sailors leap overboard and become dolphins, the hymn's central transformation.

analysis.text: The hymn shows mortals punished for failing to recognise a god, while the one who recognises him is rewarded. Dionysus' power is shown through wine, vines and wild beasts.
Tyrsenian pirates reflect Greek fear of Etruscan sea raiders. The story also explains the dolphin as a former man and affirms Dionysus' divine standing.

legacy.text: The pirates-turned-dolphins tale was retold by Ovid in the Metamorphoses and was a favourite subject in Greek art, notably the cup by Exekias showing Dionysus sailing with dolphins.

fun_facts.text: The Exekias cup (c. 530 BC) shows a vine growing from the ship's mast with dolphins around it, matching this hymn's imagery.

language_notes.text: Tyrsenian is the older spelling of Tyrrhenian, meaning Etruscan; Greeks often called Tyrrhenians pirates. The number 2530 is a stray line or page marker from the edition.
Heaven-nurtured means raised under the care of the gods; the pirates take him for a royal prince worth a ransom.
Withes are tough, flexible twigs or branches used as bands for tying.
Chid is the old past tense of chide, meaning scolded or rebuked.
Sheets are the ropes that control the angle of the sails, not cloth.
Hyperboreans were a legendary people living far north, beyond the north wind. The master lists distant places to mock the stranger's importance.
"Sheets" are ropes attached to the corners of a sail to adjust it, not cloth; hauling them taut trims the sail to the wind.
Thole-pins are pegs set in the ship's side that hold the oars in place when rowing.
"Bemused" here means bewildered or stupefied with fear, not amused.
The "..." marks a gap in the surviving text; a word or phrase, probably an address to the helmsman, is lost.
"Bare" is old past tense of "bear": Semele bore him. Zeus is the Greek name for the king of the gods.

context_notes.text: Dionysus is the god of wine, revelry and transformation. His mother Semele was a mortal woman, and his father was Zeus.
The helmsman names Zeus, Apollo and Poseidon as the gods the stranger might be. They are major Olympians of sky, music and archery, and sea.
The crew are pirates who had seized the disguised god, intending to sell him or hold him for ransom, so their change of heart comes from fear.
The helmsman alone had recognised the god's divinity earlier and urged the crew to release him, which is why he is called right-minded.
Semele, daughter of Cadmus, king of Thebes, was Dionysus' mortal mother; Zeus fathered him, making Dionysus a god born of a human woman.

literary_notes.text: The 'miserable doom' tells the audience at once that the pirates' crime will bring them ruin.
The falling bonds and calm smile show Dionysus's divine power and ease, in contrast to the pirates' ignorance.
The master expects the captive to reveal his wealth, but the audience knows he is a god and will punish them.
Streaming wine and a heavenly fragrance appeal to taste and smell, showing Dionysus' domain and marking the start of the miracle.
The lion and bear show the god's wild, dangerous side, contrasting with the pleasant gifts of wine and vines just before.
The sailors flee a fate they call miserable, yet escape into the sea and become dolphins, a transformation that is also a punishment.
Dionysus appears both merciful and terrible: he spares the loyal helmsman and makes him happy, rewarding piety.
The poet turns from the story to address the god directly, as the hymn's closing salutation.
